title: Appellant v. EBRDAT, EBRDAT 2022-AT-01 Jurisdiction Decision
text:
THE ADMINISTRATIVE TRIBUNAL
OF THE
EUROPEAN BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
Case No. 2022/AT/01
Appellant
vs.
European Bank for Reconstruction and Development
DECISION ON JURISDICTION
by the Administrative Tribunal in plenum
22 March 2022

I. Introduction
1. With the present Appeal, the Appellant requests a judicial review of the provisions of the
internal law of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (“Bank”) on leave, in
particular regarding the rules on parental leave.
2. In a prior appeal by this same Appellant, the Tribunal had rendered a decision in August
2021. In that decision, the Tribunal rejected the Appellant’s request to direct the Bank’s President
to refer his case to the Administrative Review Committee.
3. As a preliminary issue in the instant appeal, the Bank seeks to challenge the jurisdiction of
the Tribunal, arguing that, on the one hand, the subject brought before the Tribunal is a res
judicata, and, on the other hand, that the appeal is time-barred.
II. Facts and procedural background
4. On 3 November 2020, the Appellant and his HR Business Partner discussed issues related
to his forthcoming fatherhood of twins by way of surrogacy, including his potential leave
entitlements. The Appellant had a number of queries to which his HR Business Partner indicated
she would look into and follow up with the respective clarifications.
5. In an extensive exchange of emails, a dispute arose about contents and application of the
Bank’s internal rules on parental leave in the Appellant’s specific circumstances. In an email of 4
January 2021, the Appellant was informed that he had “recourse under the Administrative Review
Process should [he] wish to pursue the matter further.” In another email of 17 February 2021, the
Appellant was advised that in case of disagreement he “may search further review as set out in
Section IV, paragraph 6.4 of the ARP Directive.”
2

6. On 14 April 2021, the Appellant submitted such a request to the Bank’s President. On 5
May 2021, the President responded to the request informing the Appellant that she considered it
inadmissible. On 11 June 2021, the Appellant submitted an appeal to the Tribunal. In that appeal,
he requested to overturn the contested decision by the Bank’s President, and to direct her to refer
his case to the Administrative Review Committee.
7. In its decision of 26 August 2021 in case no. 2021/AT/02 (“Initial decision”), the Tribunal
clarified that the Appellant seeks to call into question the Bank’s internal rules on parental leave
as such, rather than contesting an individual administrative decision in his specific case. The
Tribunal determined the consequences as follows:
“57. … the subject of dispute in the current case is the Bank’s internal rules on parental
leave, namely the distinctions drawn between paid maternity leave and surrogacy leave.
These rules are incorporated in the Bank’s Leave Directive of 1 April 2019.
58. Due to its nature as a Directive, the respective set of norms, pursuant to Section IV,
paragraph 2 of the Directive on General Provisions and Glossary of Terms for the Staff
Handbook, meets the definition of a Regulatory Decision taken by the President, the Board
of Directors or the Board of Governors.
59. Pursuant to Section IV, paragraph 3 (c) of the ARP Directive such type of
Regulatory Decisions is not subject to the Administrative Review Process.
60. As the provisions of the Leave Directive are not subject to the Administrative Review
Process, a respective request for such a review is inadmissible.
61. It follows from the above that the contested decision of 5 May 2021 rightfully
rejected the Appellant’s request for administrative review as inadmissible, regardless of
its reasoning. However, the inadmissibility follows directly from the Bank’s internal law
(see above paragraph 59) rather than from its application in the contested decision.”
Regarding the admissibility of the Appellant’s mere request for referral to an Administrative
Review Committee, the Tribunal held:
“62. It has to be reiterated that the Appellant requests the Tribunal to direct the
President to refer his case to an ARC. As demonstrated above, the provisions of the Leave
3

Directive are not open to an ARP. Therefore, as the request for an ARP is inadmissible, a
referral to the ARC as an integral part of the ARP is excluded. The Appellant’s request
must fail.
63. The Tribunal is aware of its competence to review the provisions of the Bank’s
Directives, including the Leave Directive, as foreseen in Section IV, paragraph 3 (d) of the
ARP Directive. However, the Appellant has not submitted any such request. By contrast,
as reiterated above, he has limited his request to a procedural measure, without asking the
Tribunal to look into the substantial merits of his complaint of allegedly being treated
unequally without justification. Also, the Tribunal notes that in his appeal before the
Tribunal, the Appellant does not even present and/or submit substantial arguments with
respect to the alleged unjustified equal treatment.
64. Pursuant to the general principle of ne ultra petita, a tribunal may not go beyond
the pleadings of a party when considering a case. Since the Appellant’s unambiguous
request does not cover an inquiry into the substantial merits, the Tribunal is prevented
from any respective review.”
Finally, the Tribunal noted with concern that the Appellant was twice misinformed and misled
about the correct way to express his disagreement when wrongly advising him in both messages
of 4 January 2021 and of 17 February 2021 to make use of the ARP although this channel was not
open to him.
8. The present Appeal was lodged on 3 January 2022. The Appellant requests that “the
Tribunal recommend a review of the provisions contained in the Bank’s Leave Directive, Chapter
IV ‘Parental Leave’, with view to avoiding and eliminating circumstances in which staff members
are subject to unjustified unequal treatment, specifically in cases of twin and multiple births”.
9. The Tribunal directed the Bank to provide its Response to the Statement of Appeal by email
of 20 January 2022.
10. On 8 February 2022, the Bank filed a submission challenging the Tribunal’s jurisdiction.
The Appellant submitted a reply on 28 February 2022.
4

III. The Bank’s position
11. The Bank challenges the jurisdiction of the Tribunal on two independent grounds.
12. Referring to generally recognized principles of international administrative law and the
jurisprudence of various international tribunals, the Bank submits, firstly, the Appeal should be
dismissed “as the arguments and claims raised …have been decided upon by this Tribunal and
have the force of res judicata.” Challenge to Jurisdiction at 7. The Bank alleges that “the substance
of the present appeal is the same as in the initial appeal insofar as the Appellant continues to allege
that he is being subject to unequal treatment under the Bank’s Leave Directive.” Id. at 31. Pursuant
to the Bank’s view, the Appellant intends to re-litigate the same matters already decided upon. For
the Bank, it is not the role of the internal justice system to provide a Staff Member, “who has failed
to properly plead his case in the first instance, a second opportunity to do so.” Id. at 32.
13. Notwithstanding the above, the Bank argues that the appeal is time-barred. In its view, any
challenge to a regulatory decision taken pursuant to Section IV, paragraph 3 (c) (iii) of the
Directive on the Administrative Review Process, including the Leave Directive, “must be lodged
within 60 days from the date that such administrative decision was rendered.” Id. at 38. Since the
respective rules were introduced in 2018 and replicated in 2019, in the Bank’s view, the present
challenge is time-barred. Even if the time limit should start from the date of the Tribunal’s initial
decision, i.e. 26 August 2021, the deadline would have expired in November 2021.
14. The Bank emphasizes the importance to adhere to time limits. It maintains that a different
view on the application of the 60 day time limit with respect to regulatory decisions would render
time limits within the Bank’s internal justice system without any purpose as it would suggest that
a staff member could challenge any regulatory decision at any time. The Bank considers that this
would not only go against the requirements set out in the Appeals Directive but would also be
contrary to the spirit of those rules and the equitable purpose of time limits.
5

IV. The Appellant’s position
15. Pursuant to the Appellant, the initial decision and the present appeal deal with two different
matters. Whereas the decision of 26 August 2021 addresses a procedural question, the present
appeal relates to a regulatory decision with provisions which were only included in April and
October 2021.
16. Further, the Appellant points out that in the present case, no Administrative Review
Decision was made. Therefore, in his opinion, the 60 day time limit for appeals to the Tribunal
which is established in the Bank’s internal law cannot be applied. In addition, any such time limit
would oblige staff members to speculatively challenge any decision that may (or not) impact them
individually in the future through an appeal to the Administrative Tribunal.
17. Finally, the Appellant contends that even in case of the application of a time limit, there
were unique and justifiable grounds for a delay, since he had been misled by the Bank about the
correct way to express his disagreement regarding the grant of parental leave in his specific case.
V. The Tribunal’s evaluation
a) Oral hearing
18. Pursuant to Section IV, paragraph 4.03 (a) of the Bank’s Directive on the Appeals Process
(DIR/2021/28 - “Appeals Directive”), the Tribunal may of its own initiative determine that it
would be appropriate to conduct a preliminary hearing on the issue of jurisdiction. Since the parties
had ample opportunity to submit their views in writing, the Tribunal is in a position to decide the
issue of jurisdiction on the basis of the written pleadings and sees no reason to call for a preliminary
hearing in the present case.
6

b) Anonymity
19. The Appellant requests to remain anonymous, and the Bank does not oppose this request.
The Tribunal grants this request, recalling that it is inherent to an appeal process that certain facts
and opinions become known, both inside and outside the Bank. This being said, it is the Tribunal’s
established approach to limit to the maximum extent possible, inter alia, the exposure of facts or
descriptions that may identify participants of the process.
c) Merits
1. Applicable law
20. Pursuant to Section IV, paragraph 3.02 of the Appeals Directive, in considering the Appeal,
the Tribunal shall base its decision inter alia on generally recognized principles of international
administrative law. Res judicata, as a general principle of procedural law, forms part of these
principles since long; it may be defined as “Rule that final judgment or decree on merits by court
of competent jurisdiction is conclusive of rights of parties or their privies in all later suits on points
and matters determined in former suit”, requiring “identity in thing sued for as well as identity of
cause of action, of persons and parties to action, and of quality in persons for or against whom
claim is made.” (Black’s Law Dictionary, 4th edition, at 1470).
21. Section IV, paragraph 4.03 (a) of the Appeals Directive reads:
“A Statement of Appeal must be submitted to the Tribunal within sixty days of the date of
the Administrative Review Decision rendered in accordance with Section IV, paragraph
6.4.3 of the Directive on the Administrative Review Process.”
7

2. Res judicata
22. Given the fundamental requirements for the application of the principle of res judicata,
there may be no doubt that in the present case the parties are identical with the parties in the initial
decision.
23. Also, the Tribunal is aware of the fact that in both cases, the Bank’s internal rules on
parental leave are at stake.
24. However, the initial decision had a limited scope. Based on the unambiguous wording of
the appeal, the initial decision could and did only make final findings on the Appellant’s request
to have his case referred to an Administrative Review Committee. Thus, since the effects of the
initial decisions are limited to procedural matters, no decision on the merits of the Appellant’s
claim of being subject to unjustified unequal treatment was taken.
25. Therefore, the present appeal is no re-litigation of substantial matters that have already
been decided upon in the Tribunal´s initial decision. It has to be recalled that, in the initial decision,
no single word is spent on the legality of the Bank’s internal rules on parental leave. There is no
identity of subject of dispute in both cases.
26. Finally, it has to be reiterated that the Appellant’s failure, in the Bank’s words, “to properly
plead his case in the first instance” was obviously induced by the Bank’s misleading messages of
4 January 2021 and 17 February 2021 (see above paragraph 5). It would be unfair if the Bank
would now profit from its own wrongful advice at an earlier stage of the dispute.
27. It follows that the Bank’s argument of res judicata must fail.
8

3. Timeliness of the appeal
28. At the outset, the Tribunal would like to confirm its adherence to the recognized principle
of international administrative law that time limits must be observed strictly. They are
indispensable tools for all stakeholders with a view to a smooth functioning for both the
administration and the judiciary. Therefore, pursuant to Rule 6.02 (a) of the Tribunal Appeals
Procedure, a challenge to jurisdiction of the Tribunal may be based on the claim that an appeal is
time-barred.
29. However, the application of any such time limit is only possible where it is properly
established by statutory law. Since time limits provide for a limitation to procedural rights with
serious preclusive effects on the implementation of substantial rights, they must be unambiguously
established in the law.
30. In this respect, Section IV, paragraph 4.03 (a) of the Appeals Directive, prescribes that a
60 day time limit for filing an appeal starts to run from“ the date of the Administrative Review
Decision rendered in accordance with Section IV, paragraph 6.4.3 of the Directive on the
Administrative Review Process”.
31. The Tribunal takes note that no such Administrative Review Decision was rendered in the
present proceedings. Since the subject of dispute is a regulatory decision within the meaning of
Section IV, paragraph 3 (c) and (d) of the Directive on the Administrative Review Process (“ARP
Directive”), there are no appropriate channels for administrative review of such decisions and no
requirement to exhaust such channels prior to recourse to the Tribunal.
32. Further, the Tribunal notes that no other time limits for filing an appeal from a regulatory
decision can be found in the Appeals Directive.
33. To the Tribunal’s best knowledge, the Appeals Directive does not contain an explicit time
limit for an appeal against regulatory decisions that are not open to administrative review. The
Tribunal considers that an analogous application of the 60 day time limit in Section IV, paragraph
9

4.03 (a) of the Appeals Procedure is inappropriate as it would include an intervention in procedural
rights and, as such, would contradict the principle of in dubio pro libertate.
34. In light of the above, the Tribunal cannot consider the appeal as time-barred.
VI. Conclusion
36. It follows from the above, that both arguments submitted in support of the challenge to
jurisdiction are unfounded.
VII. Decision
37. The Bank’s challenge to jurisdiction is rejected.
